Tate Modern. Located in London in a converted power station on the Thames, Tate Modern opened in 2000 and is the world's leading museum of modern and contemporary art outside the United States. It houses over seventy thousand works and has transformed both the institutional museum and London's South Bank into a major cultural destination. The museum is housed in the Bankside Power Station, a nineteen-fifty industrial building redesigned by Herzog and de Meuron. The conversion preserves the industrial aesthetic while creating sophisticated gallery spaces for twentieth and twenty-first-century art. The iconic Turbine Hall, a soaring entrance space that originally housed generators, now serves as a dynamic venue for large-scale contemporary installations and performance art. The museum is strong in European Modernism, Russian Constructivism, Surrealism, and Abstract Expressionism. It has also been pioneering in establishing global and non-Western contemporary art as central to its mission rather than peripheral. The decision to offer free admission to permanent collections established Tate Modern as a public institution for broad audiences, a model followed worldwide after its remarkable success. When it opened, the museum also opened the Millennium Bridge, a pedestrian suspension bridge designed by Norman Foster and Anthony Caro, connecting Tate Modern to Saint Paul's Cathedral and fundamentally remaking London's riverfront as a cultural axis. The Switch House extension by Herzog and de Meuron, completed in 2016, added sixty percent more gallery space and established Tate Modern as the world's most visited modern art museum. It became symbolic of post-industrial cultural regeneration and contemporary urban renewal, influencing how museums approach rehabilitation of industrial sites globally.
